blocks.text: A gardener walks in holding a cloth over a 4 cm cut on the back of his hand, sustained while pruning a hedge two hours ago. He wants it 'glued up' and to go home. Before you close anything, you must know what lies beneath the wound, whether he is protected against tetanus and what he can safely take for the pain.

blocks.markdown: Minor injuries make up a large share of emergency department attendances. They are 'minor' only when the assessment has excluded a hidden serious injury. The approach has three linked parts: **wound assessment and closure**, **tetanus prophylaxis**, and **analgesia**, with recognition of the features that need **specialist referral**.

items: History: mechanism, time since injury, contamination (soil, saliva, sea or fresh water), tetanus status, allergies, handedness, occupation, anticoagulants, diabetes and other factors that impair healing.
Examination before any anaesthetic: document sensation, capillary refill, and the function of tendons and nerves distal to the wound.
Explore the wound under good light and in a bloodless field for depth, tendon, joint involvement or foreign body; image with X-ray if glass or bone injury is suspected.
Anaesthetise, irrigate with tap water or saline, and remove devitalised tissue.
Choose closure, dress, give aftercare advice and document.

rows: Clean, low-tension, straight lacerations, especially on the face or scalp
Not for wounds over joints with tension, or near the eyes; keep dry
Skin must be dry; poor in hairy or moist areas
Need anaesthetic and removal at a site-specific interval
Heavily contaminated, bites, old wounds, puncture wounds
blocks.caption: Wound closure options; local protocols specify suture materials and removal times

blocks.title: Contamination and timing
blocks.text: Closing a dirty wound can trap bacteria and cause infection, so contaminated wounds, animal and human bites, and wounds presenting late are often left open after thorough cleaning, with antibiotics considered according to local guidelines. A clean wound seen soon after injury is much more suitable for primary closure.

blocks.title: Assessing a hand laceration
blocks.prompt: The gardener has a 4 cm laceration on the back of his right hand. Describe your assessment and how it changes management.

steps.text: Examine function first: ask him to extend and flex each finger against resistance and test sensation in each digit before any anaesthetic. A finger that cannot extend suggests extensor tendon division, which needs repair or hand surgery referral.
Explore the wound through the full range of movement because a tendon laceration may be visible only when the finger is in the position it was in at injury.
Wounds from thorns or soil are contaminated and may contain plant material that X-ray may not show; irrigate generously and remove foreign material.
If tendons and nerves are intact and the wound is clean, close with sutures after local anaesthetic. If a tendon is divided or a joint entered, dress and refer to the hand surgery team.
Check tetanus status (see below) and give wound care advice and review arrangements.

blocks.answer: Document sensation and tendon function first; explore; irrigate; close if superficial and clean, refer if tendon, nerve or joint involvement.

blocks.markdown: **Tetanus prophylaxis.** Tetanus is caused by *Clostridium tetani* spores that enter wounds and produce a neurotoxin causing muscle spasm. Prophylaxis depends on the wound and the patient's immunisation history. Wounds are **tetanus-prone** if contaminated with soil or manure, if they contain foreign material or dead tissue, or are puncture wounds, bites or burns; the UK Green Book (Public Health guidance) sets the exact rules. In general, a patient who is fully immunised needs no further dose for most wounds; one with an incomplete or unknown history needs a booster of tetanus-containing vaccine and, for a tetanus-prone or high-risk wound, **human tetanus immunoglobulin** as well, and a course completed. Check the current Green Book and local policy.

**Analgesia.** Pain relief is stepwise, as in the WHO analgesic ladder: step 1, non-opioids (paracetamol and, if there are no contraindications, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug); step 2, add a weak opioid; step 3, a strong opioid titrated to effect. Match the step to severity, reassess often, give early analgesia in fractures, and use non-drug measures such as splinting, elevation and ice. **Local anaesthesia** with lidocaine blocks pain for wound care. Toxic effects (perioral tingling, confusion, seizures, arrhythmia) arise if the maximum dose is exceeded or the drug enters a vessel, so aspirate before injecting and calculate the dose. The commonly taught maximum for plain lidocaine is 3 mg/kg (check the BNF or local guidance).

blocks.caption: A 1% solution contains 1 g in 100 mL, which is 10 mg/mL

blocks.title: Maximum volume of lidocaine
blocks.prompt: Calculate the maximum volume of plain 1% lidocaine for a 70 kg adult using 3 mg/kg (check BNF or local guidance).

steps.text: Maximum dose = 3 mg/kg x 70 kg = 210 mg.

Use less if possible, and recalculate for lower weights or other concentrations; adrenaline-containing preparations have different limits and are avoided at end-arteries such as fingers by convention.

blocks.answer: 21 mL of 1% plain lidocaine (check the maximum with the BNF or local guidance).

rows: Respect the maximum daily dose; reduced dosing in low weight or liver disease
Avoid in peptic ulcer, renal impairment, asthma sensitivity and with ACE inhibitors
Respiratory depression, monitor sedation and breathing
blocks.caption: Stepwise analgesia (doses to be checked in the BNF and local guidance)

blocks.title: Red flags for specialist referral
blocks.text: Refer open fractures, wounds with tendon, nerve, vessel or joint involvement, high-pressure injection injuries, suspected compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion to injury and worse on passive stretch), septic arthritis, deep or complex hand injuries, scaphoid injury suspected despite normal X-ray, and wounds that may be non-accidental. Do not close a wound over a missed foreign body or fracture.

points: Assess before you close: examine function, explore and irrigate; avoid primary closure of contaminated wounds, bites and late presentations.
Tetanus prophylaxis depends on the wound and immunisation history: vaccine, and human tetanus immunoglobulin for high-risk wounds in the inadequately immunised.
Analgesia is stepwise, titrated and reassessed; calculate local anaesthetic doses (3 mg/kg plain lidocaine as generally taught).
Know the red flags that mandate specialist referral.

questions.stem: Which of the following wounds is generally best left open after thorough irrigation rather than closed primarily?

options.text: A cat bite puncture wound on the forearm
A clean 2 cm forehead laceration after a fall one hour ago
A clean 3 cm scalp laceration after a minor fall two hours ago
A clean superficial cut from a kitchen knife seen within an hour

questions.correctOptionText: A cat bite puncture wound on the forearm

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bite and puncture wounds are contaminated and prone to infection if closed.
distractorRationale.b: A clean, recent facial laceration is suitable for primary closure.
distractorRationale.c: A clean scalp wound is suitable for closure.
distractorRationale.d: A clean, recent superficial wound is suitable for closure.

questions.explanation: Bite and puncture wounds are deep, narrow and contaminated with oral flora, so closing them traps bacteria. They are irrigated, left open and treated according to local antibiotic guidance, while clean recent lacerations can usually be closed.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old farm worker who has never been vaccinated against tetanus presents with a deep puncture wound from a rusty fork contaminated with manure. According to UK Green Book principles as generally taught, what is the appropriate tetanus management?

options.text: Tetanus-containing vaccine and human tetanus immunoglobulin, with a plan to complete the course
No treatment since the wound is small
Antibiotics alone
Tetanus immunoglobulin alone, with no vaccine

questions.correctOptionText: Tetanus-containing vaccine and human tetanus immunoglobulin, with a plan to complete the course

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a tetanus-prone, high-risk wound in an unimmunised patient needs active and passive immunisation.
distractorRationale.b: Size does not determine tetanus risk; contamination does.
distractorRationale.d: Immunoglobulin gives only temporary passive cover; the vaccine course must also be started.

questions.explanation: Soil and manure contamination with a puncture mechanism makes the wound tetanus-prone, and an unimmunised patient lacks protective antibody. Active vaccination plus passive immunoglobulin is given, with the schedule checked in the current Green Book.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has a 3 cm laceration across the palm of his left hand after cutting a bottle. What should be done before local anaesthetic is infiltrated?

options.text: Test and document sensation and tendon function distal to the wound
Close the wound immediately
Apply a tourniquet for an hour
Omit the examination because the cut is small

questions.correctOptionText: Test and document sensation and tendon function distal to the wound

distractorRationale.a: Correct: neurovascular and tendon function must be recorded before anaesthesia, which would otherwise mask deficits.
distractorRationale.b: Closure before assessment risks missing a tendon or nerve injury and a foreign body.
distractorRationale.d: Small skin wounds can hide serious deep injuries.

questions.explanation: Anaesthetic blocks sensation and may impair examination, so function is documented first. A deficit changes management and has medicolegal importance; glass also warrants X-ray for retained fragments.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with an inversion ankle sprain, no other injuries and no medical conditions has mild to moderate pain. Which first-step analgesia fits the stepwise approach?

options.text: Paracetamol, with an NSAID such as ibuprofen if no contraindication, plus rest, ice and elevation
Intravenous morphine
No analgesia until X-ray results
Oral strong opioid as the first choice

questions.correctOptionText: Paracetamol, with an NSAID such as ibuprofen if no contraindication, plus rest, ice and elevation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: step 1 non-opioids suit mild to moderate musculoskeletal pain.
distractorRationale.b: Strong opioids are reserved for severe pain not controlled by lower steps.
distractorRationale.c: Analgesia should not be delayed for investigations.
distractorRationale.d: Starting at the top of the ladder is unnecessary for mild to moderate pain.

questions.explanation: The stepwise approach starts with the least risky effective analgesics. Mild to moderate musculoskeletal pain responds to paracetamol and an NSAID, with non-drug measures; doses are checked against the BNF.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with chronic kidney disease who takes an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic has a wrist injury. Which analgesic is best avoided?

options.text: An NSAID such as ibuprofen
Paracetamol
Splinting and elevation
A low-dose opioid titrated carefully if needed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: NSAIDs with an ACE inhibitor and diuretic raise the risk of acute kidney injury in chronic kidney disease.
distractorRationale.b: Paracetamol is usually appropriate at the correct dose.
distractorRationale.c: Non-drug measures are safe and helpful.
distractorRationale.d: Opioids may be used with caution at low doses.

questions.explanation: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin-mediated blood flow, and combined with an ACE inhibitor and diuretic the risk of kidney injury is significant. Choose another step-1 or step-2 option and check the BNF for cautions.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, and the initial wrist X-ray is normal. What is the best management?

options.text: Treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture with immobilisation and arrange further imaging or specialist review
Discharge with no follow-up because the X-ray is normal
Apply a bandage and advise return to sport
Give antibiotics

questions.correctOptionText: Treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture with immobilisation and arrange further imaging or specialist review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: scaphoid fractures can be occult on early films and risk non-union or avascular necrosis.
distractorRationale.b: A normal initial X-ray does not exclude scaphoid fracture.
distractorRationale.c: Early return to activity risks displacement.

questions.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand suggests scaphoid injury. Because early radiographs miss some fractures and the bone has a tenuous blood supply, immobilisation and follow-up imaging or review are needed.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with a tibial fracture treated in a plaster cast has increasing severe pain unrelieved by opioids, which is worse on passive stretching of the toes, and tense swelling of the calf. What is the most important action?

options.text: Urgent orthopaedic referral for suspected compartment syndrome, after loosening or releasing the cast
Give more oral analgesia and discharge
Arrange a routine clinic appointment
Reassure that pain is normal after fractures

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent orthopaedic referral for suspected compartment syndrome, after loosening or releasing the cast

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch suggest compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency.
distractorRationale.b: Analgesia alone would delay time-critical fasciotomy.
distractorRationale.d: Reassurance risks irreversible muscle and nerve damage.

questions.explanation: Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromises perfusion and can cause permanent damage within hours. Pain unrelieved by analgesia and worse on passive stretch is the key early sign, and urgent surgical review is required.

questions.stem: Using a maximum plain lidocaine dose of 3 mg/kg (check the BNF or local guidance), calculate the maximum volume of 2% lidocaine (20 mg/mL) for a 60 kg adult. Give your answer in mL.
questions.explanation: Maximum dose is 3 mg/kg x 60 kg = 180 mg. A 2% solution contains 20 mg/mL, so the volume is 180 / 20 = 9 mL. Using a 2% solution gives a smaller volume than a 1% solution for the same dose, so the concentration must always be checked.

questions.stem: Describe how you would assess and manage a 3 cm laceration on the shin of a 50-year-old man presenting 4 hours after cutting himself on a garden spade, including tetanus considerations.
markingGuide: Takes history: mechanism, time, contamination, tetanus status, allergies, anticoagulants and diabetes.
Examines distal neurovascular status and tendon function before anaesthesia, and explores for foreign body or bone involvement.
Anaesthetises (calculating dose), irrigates and debrides devitalised tissue.
Considers contamination and delay in deciding between primary closure and leaving open, with antibiotics per local guideline.
Considers tetanus-prone status (soil contamination) and gives vaccine and, if high risk and inadequately immunised, human tetanus immunoglobulin per Green Book.
Provides dressing, wound care advice and follow-up.
questions.explanation: Assessment and cleaning determine whether closure is safe. Tetanus prophylaxis depends on both the wound and the patient's immunisation history.

questions.stem: Describe the stepwise approach to analgesia for acute pain, and list injury features that should prompt specialist referral.
markingGuide: Assesses pain severity and matches analgesia to it, reassessing regularly.
Step 1: paracetamol and an NSAID if not contraindicated; Step 2: weak opioid; Step 3: strong opioid titrated, with monitoring for sedation and respiratory depression.
Uses non-drug measures such as splinting, elevation and ice and local anaesthesia where appropriate.
Identifies contraindications and cautions (renal impairment, peptic ulcer, anticoagulants, asthma).
Referral features: open fracture, tendon, nerve, vessel or joint involvement, suspected compartment syndrome, scaphoid injury, high-pressure injection injury, septic joint, non-accidental injury.
Notes that doses are checked in the BNF and local guidance.
questions.explanation: Stepwise analgesia gives effective relief with the least risk. Recognition of red-flag injuries ensures time-critical problems are not treated as minor.
